lesson.title: Combining DNA Across Species: Recombinant DNA Technology
lesson.summary: Recombinant DNA technology is the broader practice of joining DNA from different sources into a single molecule, using the same restriction enzyme and ligase based process as DNA cloning, applied to produce real medical and agricultural products.
lesson.body:
Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by joining together genetic material from two or more different sources into a combination that would not occur in nature on its own. It is worth being clear that this is not a new mechanism separate from what has already been covered: recombinant DNA technology uses exactly the same pipeline as DNA cloning, cutting with a restriction enzyme, joining with DNA ligase, inserting into a vector, and transforming into a host cell, just applied with the explicit goal of deliberately mixing genetic material across organisms, often specifically in order to produce something useful rather than simply to make extra copies of a gene for study.

The classic example is human insulin. The gene for human insulin is, obviously, human, and bacteria have no natural reason to make it. Scientists inserted the human insulin gene into a plasmid and transformed it into E. coli. Because the genetic code and the basic machinery of transcription and translation are shared across essentially all life, the bacteria correctly read the human gene and manufacture fully functional human insulin protein. This recombinant human insulin, marketed as Humulin, became the first recombinant DNA drug approved by the FDA, in 1982, replacing insulin that had previously been purified directly from the pancreases of pigs and cows.

The same basic strategy has since been extended well beyond insulin: producing other therapeutic proteins such as human growth hormone and clotting factors, engineering crops with genes for pest resistance or herbicide tolerance, manufacturing vaccine components, and building the viral vectors used in gene therapy. The details of any given application vary, but the underlying molecular logic is the one already covered.

Stepping back across this whole biotechnology sequence, the throughline is a single consistent set of tools resting on the same underlying chemistry: restriction enzymes cut DNA at predictable sites, gel electrophoresis checks fragment sizes, PCR amplifies a chosen sequence, and DNA ligase together with a vector and a host cell combines and clones DNA from different sources into something new. Every one of those tools ultimately depends on the same simple, reliable fact established all the way back at the start, that DNA follows strict, predictable base pairing rules within its double helix.
